name: Sikkim
tagline: Kangchenjunga, gompas and the high lakes
meta_description: Plan Sikkim: Gangtok, Tsomgo Lake, Lachung and Yumthang, Gurudongmar, Pelling, Yuksom and Zuluk, with permits, costs and saver, comfort and signature trips.
summary: Sikkim is India's second-smallest state, a steep wedge between Nepal, Tibet and Bhutan that climbs from 300 m on the Teesta to Kangchenjunga at 8,586 m. Come for Gangtok, the monasteries of Pelling and Yuksom, and the permit-only high lakes of the north and east. Go March to May or October to December; plan seven to ten nights.
intro: Sikkim covers about 7,100 sq km, yet within it the land rises from subtropical valleys near Rangpo to glaciers and peaks above 8,000 m. The Teesta and its tributaries cut the state into deep north–south valleys, and almost every road follows a river before climbing a ridge. Distances look short on the map and take all day on the ground.

Gangtok, the capital at about 1,650 m, is where most trips begin. It has been the seat of government since 1894, when the Chogyal moved his court from Tumlong. From here roads run east to Tsomgo Lake and the Nathu La, north up the Teesta to the valleys of Lachung and Lachen, and west over the hills to Ravangla, Pelling and Yuksom, the old royal heartland facing Kangchenjunga.

Four peoples shape the hive. The Lepchas, who call themselves Rong, are counted as the earliest inhabitants. The Bhutias arrived from Tibet and brought the Namgyal kings and the Nyingma monasteries. Limbus share the west with Nepal, and Nepali-speaking communities, who settled in large numbers from the 19th century, now form the majority and give the state its common language.

Sikkim also runs itself differently from most of India. Plastic bags were banned in 1998, farming is certified organic, and the high valleys of Lachung and Lachen still govern themselves through a village council called the Dzumsa. Much of the north and east is permit country near an international border, so the way you travel, and with whom, matters more here than almost anywhere else in the Himalaya.

story.title: From the valley of rice to the organic state

chapters.heading: Denjong, the valley of rice
chapters.text: Long before there was a kingdom, the Lepchas lived in these forests, naming every river and peak and treating Kangchenjunga as the guardian of their land. They call themselves Rong, and their own name for the country is often given as a hidden or blessed valley. Tibetans knew it as Denjong, the valley of rice, for the paddy terraces that still line the lower Teesta. The name Sikkim most likely comes from the Limbu words su and khyim, a new house or palace, said to have been used by a Limbu bride arriving in her new home. Each name records a different people who made this ground their own.

chapters.heading: Three lamas at Yuksom
chapters.text: In 1642 three Tibetan lamas met at Yuksom, in the forests of the west, and consecrated Phuntsog Namgyal as the first Chogyal, or religious king, of Sikkim. The stone seat at Norbugang where the ceremony is remembered still stands above the village, and the name Yuksom is read as the meeting place of the three lamas. The founding lama, Lhatsun Chempo, went on to establish Pemayangtse monastery in 1705. The capital moved to Rabdentse in 1670, and after raids from Bhutan and Nepal it shifted again to Tumlong and finally to Gangtok in 1894. The Namgyal dynasty ruled until 1975.

chapters.heading: Salt, wool and the Lhasa road
chapters.text: Sikkim sat on the shortest road between the plains of Bengal and Lhasa. Mule trains carried wool, salt, musk and yak tails down from Tibet and took cloth, sugar and metal goods back up, crossing the Jelep La from Kalimpong through what is now Zuluk, or the Nathu La above Tsomgo. The British made Sikkim a protectorate after the Treaty of Tumlong in 1861 and used this route for the Younghusband expedition to Tibet in 1903–04. Border trade over the Nathu La stopped in 1962 and reopened in 2006, and the old mule path above Zuluk is now sold to travellers as the Silk Route.

chapters.heading: From kingdom to organic state
chapters.text: Sikkim remained a protected kingdom under India after 1950, and in 1975 it became the 22nd state of the Indian Union after a referendum. Since then it has made choices that set it apart. Plastic bags were banned in 1998. In 2016 the state was declared fully organic, with chemical fertilisers and pesticides phased out of its farms. The same year Khangchendzonga National Park became India's first mixed natural and cultural World Heritage Site. In the high north, the Lachungpa and Lachenpa communities still settle grazing, trade and village matters through the Dzumsa, their traditional council.

highlights.title: Kangchenjunga from Pelling at dawn
highlights.text: From Pelling's ridge at about 2,100 m, the Kangchenjunga massif fills the northern sky, from Kabru to Pandim. October to December gives the clearest mornings. Pair sunrise with Pemayangtse monastery, founded in 1705, and the ruins of the old capital at Rabdentse a short walk below.

highlights.title: Tsomgo Lake and the Nathu La road
highlights.text: A permit day trip from Gangtok climbs 40 km to Tsomgo Lake at about 3,750 m, frozen in mid-winter and ringed by rhododendron in May. Indian nationals can continue to the Nathu La at 4,310 m on permitted days. Book through a registered Gangtok agency; check current status before you travel.

highlights.title: Lachung and the Yumthang valley
highlights.text: North Sikkim's best-known circuit follows the Teesta and Lachung Chu to the village of Lachung, then up to Yumthang at about 3,560 m, where the Shingba rhododendron sanctuary flowers from April to early June. It runs as a two- or three-night permit tour from Gangtok.

highlights.title: Gurudongmar, a lake above 5,000 m
highlights.text: From Lachen a pre-dawn drive crosses the Tibetan plateau edge to Gurudongmar Lake, sacred to Buddhists, Sikhs and Hindus, at over 5,100 m. It is one of the highest lakes reachable by road in India and needs careful acclimatisation. Road access has been disrupted since 2023; check current status before you travel.

highlights.title: Yuksom, where the kingdom began
highlights.text: The first Chogyal was crowned at Yuksom in 1642. Today it is a quiet village with the Norbugang coronation site, Kathok lake and Dubdi, counted as Sikkim's oldest monastery, an hour's walk uphill. It is also the trailhead for Dzongri and the Goecha La trek into Khangchendzonga National Park.

highlights.title: The zigzags above Zuluk
highlights.text: On the old Kalimpong–Lhasa mule route in East Sikkim, the road above Zuluk at about 3,000 m climbs in dozens of hairpin bends towards Thambi viewpoint and the Nathang plateau. Stay in a village homestay and watch sunrise on Kangchenjunga. Indian nationals only, by permit; check current status before you travel.

money_savers: Use the shared jeeps from Siliguri's SNT stand and Gangtok's Deorali and Vajra stands; a seat to Gangtok or Gyalshing costs a few hundred rupees against several thousand for a reserved car.
For Tsomgo Lake and North Sikkim, join a shared permit tour from a registered Gangtok agency; a seat in a shared jeep with stay and meals costs far less than reserving a vehicle for two.
Travel in March, early April or the first half of December, when Gangtok and Pelling room rates sit below the October and Durga Puja peak.
Stay in village homestays in Yuksom, Lachung or Zuluk; meals are usually included and the money stays in the village.
Eat at local canteens and momo shops off MG Marg, where a plate of momos or thukpa costs a fraction of hotel restaurant prices.
Plan west Sikkim as a loop, Gangtok to Ravangla, Pelling and Yuksom, so you never pay for a car to return empty along the same road.
getting_there: Most travellers reach Sikkim through Siliguri in West Bengal. Bagdogra Airport has direct flights from Delhi, Kolkata, Mumbai, Bengaluru and other cities, and New Jalpaiguri (NJP) is the main railway station, with overnight trains from Kolkata and Delhi. From either, Gangtok is about 120 km and 4–5 hours by road along the Teesta through the Rangpo border post, by shared jeep, SNT bus or private car. Pakyong Airport, about 30 km from Gangtok, has had only limited and irregular flights since it opened in 2018. The NH10 along the Teesta is often hit by landslides and flood damage, and traffic is sometimes routed via Kalimpong or Lava. A railway from Sevoke to Rangpo is under construction. Check current status before you travel.
permits: Foreign nationals need a Restricted Area Permit to enter Sikkim, issued free at the Rangpo and Melli check posts, at Bagdogra Airport, by Sikkim Tourism offices and online. Protected Area Permits are needed for Tsomgo Lake and the Nathu La, North Sikkim (Lachung, Yumthang, Lachen, Gurudongmar) and the Zuluk Silk Route; registered travel agents apply for them with your ID and photos. Nathu La, Gurudongmar and Zuluk have been open to Indian nationals only. Treks into Khangchendzonga National Park from Yuksom need park and trekking permits. Rules and open days change often; check current status before you travel.

months.weather: Gangtok about 4 to 13 °C; snow in the north
months.summary: Cold, dry and clear. Gangtok and Pelling have crisp mornings and long Kangchenjunga views, and hotel rates are low outside the New Year week. Tsomgo Lake is frozen, and heavy snow can close the roads to Nathu La, Yumthang and Gurudongmar for days at a time. Pack proper winter layers; most homestays have no central heating.
months.tip: Keep a spare day in any North Sikkim plan; snow closures are common in January.

months.weather: Gangtok about 6 to 15 °C; snow above 3,000 m
months.summary: Still cold, with snow on the high roads and clear skies in the middle hills. Losar, the Tibetan new year, usually falls in February or early March, and monasteries hold masked dances in the days before it. Pelling and Yuksom are quiet and cheap. North Sikkim tours run when roads are open, often only as far as Lachung.
months.tip: Ask your agency each morning whether Tsomgo and Yumthang are open; permits are issued day by day.

months.summary: Spring arrives. Rhododendrons start to flower in the middle hills, roads to the north usually reopen, and the light is still good for mountain views. Rates are fair and crowds small until the Holi week. A good month for Pelling, Yuksom and the first North Sikkim trips, with snow still lying around Yumthang and Tsomgo.
months.tip: Book Lachung for late March if you want snow at Yumthang and fewer vehicles.

months.summary: One of the best months. Rhododendron flowers spread from Ravangla up to Yumthang, Tsomgo is thawing, and treks from Yuksom are in season. School holidays from late April lift prices and fill North Sikkim permits, so book early. Haze can soften mountain views in the afternoons.
months.tip: Go to Yumthang in mid to late April for the best of the Shingba rhododendrons.

months.summary: Peak family season. Yumthang's flowers are at their height in early May, Gurudongmar is usually open, and Gangtok fills with visitors from the plains. Afternoon showers begin late in the month. Saga Dawa, the holiest month of the Buddhist year, often begins now, with a procession in Gangtok on its full moon.
months.tip: Leave Gangtok for Tsomgo by 7 am; the permit queue and traffic build quickly in May.

months.summary: The monsoon arrives in the first half of June. Rain brings landslides on the NH10 and the North Sikkim roads, and views close in. Early June is still busy with holidaymakers. Saga Dawa may fall now. Travel with buffer days and keep plans flexible.
months.tip: Build in a spare day at the end of the trip; NH10 closures can last a day or more.

months.summary: The wettest stretch. Landslides cut roads often, North Sikkim tours are frequently cancelled, and mountain views are rare. Hotels discount heavily and the forests are deep green. Only come with time to spare and a tolerance for rain and leeches on forest walks.
months.tip: If you must travel now, stay in Gangtok and the west and keep the north as optional.

months.summary: Heavy rain continues. Pang Lhabsol, honouring Kangchenjunga as Sikkim's guardian deity, can fall in late August or September. Roads remain unreliable and North Sikkim is often closed. Rates are low. Clouds clear for brief windows, mostly early in the morning.
months.tip: Carry a proper rain jacket and quick-drying shoes; umbrellas do little on mountain roads.

months.summary: The monsoon eases through the month, and late September brings the first clear mornings. Pang Lhabsol often falls this month, with warrior dances at the palace monastery in Gangtok. Landslide repairs may still be under way in the north. A quieter, cheaper time before the October peak.
months.tip: Late September is the sweet spot: autumn prices have not yet risen and the rain is mostly over.

months.summary: The best month for views. The air is washed clean after the monsoon, Kangchenjunga stands out from Pelling and Gangtok, and the high roads are open. Durga Puja and Diwali bring heavy crowds from Kolkata and the plains, and prices peak. Book stays and permit tours weeks ahead.
months.tip: Avoid arriving in the Durga Puja week unless your stays are booked; rooms and cars run short.

months.weather: Gangtok about 9 to 17 °C; dry and clear
months.summary: Clear, dry and cooler, with crowds thinning after Diwali. Long views from Pelling, Zuluk and Ravangla, and the north is open until the first heavy snow. Nights in Lachung, Lachen and Zuluk are cold. A strong month for photographers and couples.
months.tip: Carry a down jacket for Zuluk and Lachen; night temperatures can drop below freezing.

months.weather: Gangtok about 5 to 14 °C; snow likely in the north
months.summary: Cold and mostly clear. Early December is calm and good value. The Christmas and New Year weeks bring crowds to Gangtok and Pelling, and snow can close Nathu La, Yumthang and Gurudongmar. Tsomgo begins to freeze. Good for mountain views and winter light.
months.tip: For snow, plan Lachung or Tsomgo in late December, with a day spare for closures.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Sikkim?
faqs.a: March to May and October to December. Spring brings rhododendrons in Yumthang and the middle hills; autumn gives the clearest Kangchenjunga views. June to September is monsoon, with frequent landslides and closures in the north. January and February are cold but clear, though snow often shuts the high roads.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to visit Sikkim?
faqs.a: Indian nationals need no permit for Gangtok, Pelling, Yuksom and Ravangla, but need Protected Area Permits for Tsomgo, Nathu La, North Sikkim and Zuluk, arranged by registered agents. Foreign nationals need a Restricted Area Permit to enter Sikkim, plus further permits for some areas. Rules change; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do I reach Gangtok from Bagdogra or NJP?
faqs.a: Gangtok is about 120 km from Bagdogra Airport and New Jalpaiguri station, 4–5 hours by road via the Teesta valley. Shared jeeps run from Siliguri's SNT stand and from NJP, SNT buses leave Siliguri, and private taxis cost roughly ₹3,500–5,000. Landslides sometimes divert traffic via Kalimpong; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for Sikkim?
faqs.a: Seven to ten nights covers Gangtok with Tsomgo, two or three nights in North Sikkim at Lachung and Lachen, and the west at Pelling and Yuksom. With five nights, choose Gangtok plus either the north or the west. Add a spare day for landslides or snow closures, which are common.

faqs.q: Is altitude sickness a risk in Sikkim?
faqs.a: Yes in the north and east. Tsomgo is about 3,750 m, Nathu La 4,310 m and Gurudongmar over 5,100 m. Sleep in Lachen before Gurudongmar, ascend slowly, drink water and descend if you feel unwell. Children, seniors and anyone with heart or lung conditions should talk to their doctor before going.

faqs.q: Can foreigners visit Nathu La and Gurudongmar Lake?
faqs.a: Nathu La, Gurudongmar and the Zuluk Silk Route have been open only to Indian nationals. Foreigners have been permitted to visit Tsomgo Lake and Yumthang, in groups through registered agents. These rules change with security conditions; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much does a Sikkim trip cost?
faqs.a: A saver traveller using shared jeeps, shared permit tours and homestays spends about ₹2,000–3,500 a day. Comfort travel with a private car and good hotels runs about ₹7,000–12,000 per person per day. North Sikkim private tours add significantly because cars, permits and lodges are booked as a package.

faqs.q: Is Sikkim safe for solo women travellers?
faqs.a: Sikkim is widely regarded as one of India's safer states, with a calm, orderly capital. Use registered taxis and agencies, avoid driving after dark on mountain roads, and share your plans with your hotel. In remote areas like Zuluk and Lachen, stay in homestays that your agency or hotel has arranged.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network and ATM access in Sikkim?
faqs.a: Gangtok, Namchi, Gyalshing and Pelling have 4G and ATMs. Network fades above Mangan and is patchy or absent in Lachen, Lachung, Zuluk and on treks from Yuksom. Carry enough cash for the north before you leave Gangtok; card payment is rare in villages.
